items.question: Why do you think AI systems that self-improve using empirical evidence will drive further progress in the next few years?
items.object: AI systems that self-improve using empirical evidence
items.answer: Really now, I think all these things are in place. We have powerful foundation models, really powerful mutation operators, powerful selection operators, and models that can code quite well. Putting this all together means we'll have systems that self-improve based on empirical evidence that they collect in a number of hard domains. I think that's really what's going to drive further improvements in AI in the next few years.
quotes: Really now, I think all these things are in place. We have powerful foundation models, really powerful mutation operators, powerful selection operators, and models that can code quite well.
Putting this all together means we'll have systems, as I said, that self-improve based on empirical evidence that they collect in a number of hard domains.
I think that's really what's going to drive further improvements in AI in the next few years.

rubrics.text: The response argues that combining foundation models, mutation operators, selection operators, and model coding capabilities now makes empirically driven AI self-improvement possible.

items.question: How do you assess progress on the NetHack benchmark amid recent advances in AI?
items.object: The NetHack benchmark amid progress in AI
items.answer: To be absolutely honest, there's not that much progress on that NetHack benchmark, right? We have seen a lot of amazing progress in AI in terms of large language models, foundation models in general, but NetHack is still unsolved. That grand challenge is still there.
quotes: To be absolutely honest, there's not that much progress on that NetHack benchmark, right? We have seen a lot of amazing progress in AI in terms of large language models, foundation models in general, but NetHack is still unsolved. That grand challenge is still there.

items.question: How do you assess the prospects of large language models solving the NetHack challenge?
items.object: Large language models applied to the NetHack challenge
items.answer: I mean, you can try it yourself already. I think it's fair to say already LLMs are not going to crack it. It's still a very hard exploration problem, and even systems like O1 won't get us all the way.
quotes: I mean, you can try it yourself already. I think it's fair to say already LLMs are not going to crack it. It's still a very hard exploration problem, and even systems like O1 won't get us all the way.

items.question: How did you approach writing about artificial intelligence for a general audience in the 10 Things You Should Know book series?
items.object: Writing a popular science book about artificial intelligence for the 10 Things You Should Know series
items.answer:
This is a popular science book, so this is new to me as well, trying to write for a wider public audience. To me, this was an exciting project because the book itself is part of a series, 10 Things You Should Know. There are books about space and time and numbers and dinosaurs and trees, and now there's one on artificial intelligence. I think it shows you a little bit what an important topic AI has become for the public. What I found intriguing about writing such a book is that, on one hand, I think it's important to write in simple terms about why AI has taken off so much in the last 10 years, from AI for games—a lot of progress has been made with game environments like NetHack, and before that Atari, Go, and chess—but why was there such a seismic shift in the last three years with the advent of large language models? How do they work? Explaining that to someone who might not have any computer science or mathematical background, I found important to do.

But then I really couldn't resist talking about things that are dear to me right now in my research: topics around self-improvement, artificial superhuman intelligence, the automation of science, and robotics. It basically tries to do both a little bit: pick people up that haven't really heard much about AI before, but then also get very quickly to the frontier of what might be coming at them in the next few years in terms of AI progress.

items.question: How do you understand artificial superhuman intelligence in relation to the distinction between narrow and general AI?
items.object: Artificial superhuman intelligence and the distinction between narrow and general AI
items.answer:
There was a great paper from Google DeepMind published this year at ICML called “The Levels of AGI,” where the authors tried to define different levels of capability that will get us from things that are not really at the human level, towards human level, towards superhuman level. The first distinction these authors make is between narrow systems and general systems.

Within narrow domains, we already have superhuman systems. We have superhuman Go-playing AI, superhuman chess-playing AI. On the way there you have things like calculators that are maybe really helpful in a certain way, but not superhuman in the math domain. You can chart the way on narrow AI from things that are narrow and not superhuman, or not even human level, towards superhuman systems like AlphaGo.

But what we really care about more and more nowadays is having general-purpose systems. Maybe at some point people still believed that you train a superhuman Go system and maybe that system would learn something so general about exploring a hard domain that you could take something out of Go and apply it somewhere else. Even with Watson AI, there was this belief that maybe this can now be applied to the medical domain. It turns out that this is hard or even impossible: training these systems in narrow domains and hoping that they can generalize outside of them is just never going to work.

At the same time, we have now seen systems like ChatGPT, Gemini, and so on that suddenly are able to answer questions on an extremely broad range of topics. That's where the authors of this Levels of AGI paper talk about general AI and its different levels. They categorize things by how many, what percentage of average humans, a system can compete with, and what percentage of skilled humans it can compete with. At some point it can do better than any human on earth on a certain topic. For the general systems, the authors argue that with these large language models and chatbots we're basically at this emerging stage of AGI. If you go all the way up to level five, you'd get to artificial superhuman intelligence: an AI that on basically any human task is better than any human on earth. In the book I make the argument that that is feasible.

items.question: How do you view the possibility of broad generality in AI?
items.object: Broad generality in AI
items.answer: I'm not arguing that broad generality is impossible. I think we're seeing, as the authors of that paper argue as well, signs of general-purpose AI, which is what we see with chatbots nowadays.

items.question: How do you understand the role of self-play in reaching superhuman AI performance in games like Go and chess?
items.object: Self-play as a route to superhuman performance in Go and chess
items.answer: We can have this AI improve itself by playing against itself, against previous versions of itself. From that we get a bootstrapping that gets us to a system that's in an open-ended way just further and further improving itself in the domain of Go or chess, to the point where it's explored the space of strategies in this game so much that it's better than any human in the game. That gets us superhuman artificial intelligence for a narrow domain like Go or chess.

That gets you superhuman artificial intelligence for a narrow domain like Go or chess.

items.question: Why do you see foundation models as a paradigm shift that makes AGI and artificial superhuman intelligence more relevant to discuss?
items.object: The shift from narrow-domain AI to foundation models and its implications for AGI
items.answer: What happened with large language models, and why we are now starting to talk more and more about AGI and artificial superhuman intelligence, is that the paradigm shifted. We're not looking at one specific narrow domain, and we don't train these models in just one narrow domain. Instead, we're taking internet-scale textual data and image data and training a foundation model. As we can see empirically, after it's pretrained and then fine-tuned with RLHF to be more helpful and harmless, these models can pass different kinds of university entry exams, provide sensible answers for a very broad range of questions, with some caveats, hallucination and so on, and code to some extent. That's a certain generality that we've never seen with RL and self-play systems before. The question now again is, is it feasible to think these systems can further and further improve to the point where they become superhuman on many, and at some point all, of these tasks?

items.question: Why do you think foundation models offer a plausible path toward artificial superhuman intelligence?
items.object: The feasibility of artificial superhuman intelligence through open-ended self-improvement
items.answer:
We do have an existence proof of an intelligence that is general, in the sense that it can, for any kind of problem domain, set its mind to it and do really well, and that's humans. On top of that, we now have systems that have been consuming internet-scale data of text and images on the web. That gathers foundation models that are only at the level of emerging AGI, but that do encompass notions of what humans find interesting. There's a great paper called Omni and Omni-epic from Jeff Clune's lab showing that these foundation models learn what humans generally find interesting.

When you have a massive exploration space in which you want to throw an AI at it, now we have a way to massively prune down this search space. That's one thing. The other observation is that these foundation models are really good at generating variations of data. You can give it a few short prompt examples, and it can generate variations. Take these two things together: something that can generate data or variations and something that can select for what is interesting. I believe you can build very powerful open-ended self-improvement systems. It requires a third thing as well, which is connecting this process back to some source of empirical evidence. Then you have the ingredients for technological evolution, which generates variations, tries them out empirically, then selects which ones are most interesting and further selects which ones to vary. By now there are multiple papers, some from my group, building such self-improvement systems based on this recipe. With that in mind, I think it's not an extreme stretch to say we'll see more of these self-improving systems that use foundation models as the foundation but become more like an agent that collects empirical evidence by itself and tries things out.

items.question: How do you envision open-ended systems for artificial superhuman intelligence?
items.object: Open-ended systems for artificial superhuman intelligence
items.answer:
We had a position paper at ICML called “Open-Endedness Is Essential for Artificial Superhuman Intelligence.” It is building systems that are not directly optimizing for a specific task or output or outcome, but that are instead autonomously exploring problem domains, finding interesting artifacts and stepping stones that become enablers for future progress. You can run them for longer and longer, and they would accumulate more and more interesting artifacts.

The things you mentioned, LLMs, foundation models, Transformers, might be the core models that drive some of that exploration. But I think the main bulk of the work you'll see in the next few years is the kind of systems you build around such LLMs: systems that can go out there and try to collect empirical evidence for certain domains, self-improve based on that feedback, and at some point be let loose to generate an increasing wealth of interesting artifacts, whether that's research insights and explanations or data that's interesting for scientific domains.

items.question: How do you think about the autonomy implied by “letting loose” AI agents to explore?
items.object: Direction and autonomy for exploring AI agents
items.answer: I think we will be providing direction for a few reasons. One is an AI safety aspect. I don't think we want to—I mean, when I said “let loose,” that was maybe very—“let loose” is a spectrum.

items.question: How much freedom do you think self-improving AI systems should have to explore?
items.object: Human direction and freedom for self-improving AI systems
items.answer: We would want to direct them. First of all, from a safety perspective. Secondly, compute, while it's still increasing, I think we're never going to have, in the foreseeable future, the kind of endless compute we would want to really just let these self-improving systems explore all kinds of domains equally. As humans, we will have to make decisions about what we find most interesting as domains to apply such processes. But within a certain domain or question that we might have, I think we'll be giving these systems a lot of freedom.

items.question: Why do you think defining reward functions and applying reinforcement learning is insufficient for developing generally capable AI?
items.object: Reward functions as a route to generally capable AI
items.answer: It's not going to be what people believed for a long while, that we have these domains where we can define a reward function and just reinforcement learn our way towards generally capable AI. I don't think that's true. For most interesting domains we just don't have that reward function. That goes back to NetHack as well: NetHack is a great example. We don't have a reward function that tells us how to win in this game. You just have to have a system be curious, start exploring by itself, and see what it discovers. I think that's true for most domains that we find interesting.

items.question: How do you distinguish your vision of open-ended search from approaches based on intrinsic reward functions?
items.object: Open-ended search versus intrinsic reward functions
items.answer:
There was work on trying to come up with intrinsic reward functions, things like empowerment, being able to exert control in an environment, or learning generally about environment dynamics, and basically steering reinforcement learning agents towards regions in an environment where maybe they have a lot of uncertainty about how the environment or dynamics work. There are a lot of attempts at building such intrinsic reward functions that don't rely on some kind of gold-standard ground-truth reward signal that you can directly optimize for.

But I don't think that's what I'm talking about here. When you talk about reward functions, you automatically talk about forcing: you'll use that reward function to reinforce a certain behavior. What I want to see, and I think we're getting there with everything that has happened in the last two years, is models that have ways to create variations of what might be interesting to explore, then shrink down the space of things they could explore to those things that are interesting, as measured by what humans generally would find interesting. That can be done via proxy using a foundation model, and then, as I said, going out there and collecting empirical evidence to refine some of the ideas this model has. It isn't really reinforcement learning. This is really an open-ended search method. Maybe it might use reinforcement in certain bits: if it learns through empirical evidence that a certain behavior leads to interesting empirical results, then maybe I want to reinforce that behavior. But reinforcement will just be one component in this bigger system, and it's not going to be the main one.

items.question: Why do you find the prospect of AI systems making more autonomous scientific discoveries interesting?
items.object: AI systems making autonomous scientific discoveries
items.answer: First of all, AI has already been used a lot to make really fantastic scientific discoveries. Literally last week the Nobel Prize was awarded to protein folding. It's a fantastic example. But I think the future holds a time where these systems can even more autonomously make scientific discoveries. I think that's going to be really interesting, partly because if you apply that to a domain like AI itself, it becomes self-referential. It becomes not just improving a certain question or metric that you as a human define, but also improving the way it's improving along the way.

items.question: How do you see PromptBreeder's significance for automating scientific research?
items.object: PromptBreeder as a prototype for automating scientific research
items.answer: We had a research prototype for the domain of prompt engineering research that we published this year at ICML called PromptBreeder. The idea is that with large language models, a lot of the behavior of these models can be shaped by the way you prompt them. That's well known: you have prompt strategies like chain-of-thought prompting that have dramatic effects on the capabilities of these LLMs. If you change the prompt strategy—not just the question you give the model, but the kind of prompt you give before, in terms of how it should solve or decompose the question—then these models can get massively better in mathematical reasoning or coding. Wouldn't it be nice if you could automate this process? Could you have the LLM talk to itself, suggest variations of existing prompt series, empirically try them out, see if they lead to better reasoning capabilities, and evolve those further that work best? That's what we found with PromptBreeder. That's showing some automation of science in a quite narrow domain of prompt engineering, but I think it's no stretch to think about where that might lead if you scale it up further and it becomes more general.

items.question: What do you find interesting about how PromptBreeder applies evolutionary search to language?
items.object: PromptBreeder's self-referential evolutionary search over prompts
items.answer: It's an evolutionary strategy, but I think the interesting thing at this point is that we see evolutionary approaches being applied directly to language itself. That's why I said if it's talking to itself, it's suggesting variations of prompt strategies, and the way it's doing that is by being prompted by us to do it. That means the entire mechanism that defines this evolutionary search is again a prompt mechanism, and because that's true, it can be applied to itself. It can try to improve the prompts it's using to improve, to mutate prompts, and to do this evolutionary search. That's why you can make it self-referential.

items.question: Why do you think evolutionary prompt search needs to be grounded in empirical evidence?
items.object: Empirical grounding in evolutionary prompt search
items.answer: I'm not saying there's going to be no empirical evidence that guides this kind of search. I think it needs to be grounded; otherwise this system can just hallucinate to itself that it's found something really cool, and it's not helpful for us.
quotes: I'm not saying there's going to be no empirical evidence that guides this kind of search. I think it needs to be grounded; otherwise this system can just hallucinate to itself that it's found something really cool, and it's not helpful for us.

rubrics.text: The response explains that without empirical grounding, an evolutionary prompt search system can mistakenly judge itself to have made a valuable discovery.

items.question: How do you see the potential of evolutionary search in open-ended domains such as computer science, math, and AI research?
items.object: Evolutionary search in open-ended research domains
items.answer: I think it's very powerful once you have open-ended domains like computer science, math, or AI research. There's a lot of things you can explore. There were papers like FunSearch from Google DeepMind, showing you can evolve computer programs and empirically show that they work better than some of the handcrafted computer programs people have been developing.
quotes: I think it's very powerful once you have open-ended domains like computer science, math, or AI research. There's a lot of things you can explore. There were papers like FunSearch from Google DeepMind, showing you can evolve computer programs and empirically show that they work better than some of the handcrafted computer programs people have been developing.

rubrics.text: The response states that FunSearch demonstrated that evolved computer programs can empirically outperform some human-handcrafted programs.

items.question: How do you assess the AI Scientist paper by David Ha and others as a step toward AI systems doing science?
items.object: The AI Scientist paper by David Ha and others
items.answer:
I think it's a fantastic existence proof. They have all of the different ingredients I was mentioning: creating variations of data, empirically testing them out, and having some kind of loop that can improve over time. I think it's really great in that regard; it demonstrates that this is possible.

If we were to say something along the lines of levels of AI science, I think it's still very early. We can make a similar categorization of the levels you'd have to go through. Maybe there's a bachelor student level, where as a supervisor you have to double-check every experiment the student is running to make sure it's implemented correctly and the data is interpreted correctly. Then you could go up the levels to master's student, PhD student, postdoc, and maybe at some point professor that supervises multiple AI scientists. The work we're seeing in the space right now is still very early days, maybe producing workshop-paper-level quality. I think they say this in the paper as well. In the end, we have to qualitatively look at the generated papers and see if they produce interesting, valuable insights. Maybe at some point we'll get there, but there's still a lot of stuff to do.

items.question: Why do you think an automated scientific process has to use evolutionary search?
items.object: Evolutionary search in automated science
items.answer: I think it has to be evolutionary. Science is an evolutionary search. We have certain explanations of how the world works, and then people come up with variations of these or new ones. They have to live up to empirical scrutiny, and we keep those explanations that can best explain empirical evidence and that are also hard to vary, according to David Deutsch, whom I cite quite a lot in the book. In a way, science the way humans do it is already an evolutionary search for better explanations and better insights. I don't see any other way an automated scientific process can work; it has to be evolutionary as well.
quotes: I think it has to be evolutionary. Science is an evolutionary search. We have certain explanations of how the world works, and then people come up with variations of these or new ones. They have to live up to empirical scrutiny, and we keep those explanations that can best explain empirical evidence and that are also hard to vary, according to David Deutsch, whom I cite quite a lot in the book. In a way, science the way humans do it is already an evolutionary search for better explanations and better insights. I don't see any other way an automated scientific process can work; it has to be evolutionary as well.

items.question: How do you understand the relationship between evolutionary algorithms and the broader evolutionary approach emerging around foundation models?
items.object: Evolutionary computation combined with foundation models
items.answer:
I don't think they're the same. People in the evolutionary computation community probably would not be happy if I said they're the same. But I think this is a really interesting point, because it's what we're generally seeing in the field right now. People have spent decades investigating evolutionary procedures; similarly, people have spent decades doing reinforcement learning. Now we have these foundation models, and people, including people in my teams, are taking previous approaches and replacing more and more parts of them with a foundation model.

In evolution research, there are many ways people have been devising the fitness function, variation operator, or crossover operators. In PromptBreeder, and also in another paper, Rainbow Teaming, for automating jailbreaking of large language models, we ask an LM to generate a mutation of a data point or judge whether one example is more interesting than another. In some way you could say this is a massive homunculus of some aspects of an evolutionary system and some aspects of a foundation model. I think that's where the field is going.

items.question: In what sense do you regard NVIDIA's Voyager, which uses a large language model to play Minecraft, as reinforcement learning?
items.object: NVIDIA's Voyager and the meaning of reinforcement learning
items.answer:
There was a fantastic paper by NVIDIA called Voyager, where they show that a large language model can learn to play Minecraft. There's no actual reinforcement learning happening there; there are no parameter updates of that model. It's literally a large language model talking to itself about what it should explore next in Minecraft, given a goal that it selects itself. It talks to itself to write a small computer program, executes that in a Minecraft environment, and autonomously assesses whether it achieved the goal. Based on that, it takes this program and puts it in a skill library to refer to later and maybe refine or reuse.

A classical reinforcement learning researcher would say this is not reinforcement learning: there's no difference learning or policy gradient or whatever. But it is reinforcement learning in a sense that there's an environment, an agent makes observations, and based on the observations it adjusts its behavior. It's just not in the traditional sense. I think we see this in many different areas of AI and machine learning right now: now that these large language models are there and used in all kinds of places, we're turning things that were quite well-defined theoretically before into things that look a little weird but actually work extremely well empirically.

items.question: How promising do you find the approach of putting an LLM in a loop with the ability to evaluate its own output?
items.object: Using an LLM in a loop with the ability to evaluate its own output
items.answer: This has now been empirically shown in various papers: Omni and Omni-epic from Jeff Clune's lab, PromptBreeder from my lab, and FunSearch from Google DeepMind. I think we'll see much more of that recipe working really well.
quotes: This has now been empirically shown in various papers: Omni and Omni-epic from Jeff Clune's lab, PromptBreeder from my lab, and FunSearch from Google DeepMind. I think we'll see much more of that recipe working really well.

items.question: How do you think about using a language model to judge its own generated jailbreaks in Rainbow Teaming?
items.object: Rainbow Teaming and language models judging their own generated attacks
items.answer:
In Rainbow Teaming, we have taken inspiration from PromptBreeder to find adversarial attacks against large language models. Normally, if you want to deploy a foundation model or large language model, you have to make sure it's safe, so it can't easily be prompted to say harmful things or give advice about topics you shouldn't get advice about. In the past this was done mostly by humans finding such jailbreaks. We came up with a system that, again by talking to itself, proposes attacks against itself and empirically tries out whether these attacks lead to harmful responses. The harmful responses are judged by the LM itself.

There's an underlying hypothesis we see all over the place right now, which is that verification is easier than generation. If you generate a lot of possibilities and then verify them automatically, you can find really interesting artifacts evolving. That's true for Rainbow Teaming: there's literally an LM judge that judges whether one generated jailbreak is more effective than a previously generated jailbreak. If it is, we keep that and further evolve it.

At the end of the day, we still do hard-coded empirical evaluations because we want to see, after running the system for many steps, whether these jailbreaks are actually as effective as the system thinks they are. That's what we do at the end of the day: a held-out test evaluation. But the entire open-ended system is running by itself, basically by having the LM talk to itself and assess what's interesting.

items.question: Why do you find the AI debate approach in AK Khan's paper promising for overseeing highly capable AI systems?
items.object: AI debate as a method for overseeing highly capable AI systems
items.answer:
The idea is that we'll at some point live in a future where our AI systems might be more intelligent in terms of knowing more about medicine or certain domains than either an average human or even an expert human. If that future comes, there's a question of how you make sure you still have oversight over such very capable models.

There was a paper from OpenAI before that argued we should already look into this question. We shouldn't wait until we have these very capable models. The way we should be looking into these questions now is by simulating this relationship, having a weak, say, LM and a slightly stronger LM, so we can ask and investigate research questions with this setup, simulating that you have a human and then a superhuman AI.

What we wanted to investigate is whether we can already have humans in the loop. We give a human a question that's very hard to answer. We make sure it's hard for a human but maybe not for an AI by withholding information from the human. We take the QuALITY dataset, which has some fictional stories, and don't show the stories to the human. We just give the human a question and two possible answers, one correct and the other wrong. The human doesn't have any chance to answer without talking to an AI that has the context and can look at the story. But the setup is that the human can't really trust that AI, because if they talk to one AI, sometimes that AI is going to argue for the correct answer and equally likely it's going to argue for the wrong answer. By conversing with the AI over multiple turns, you can try to figure out whether it's lying or not, but it's quite difficult.

We contrast this consultancy approach with a debate approach. Instead of talking to one AI, the human talks to two AIs that debate, one for the correct and one for the wrong answer. What we show empirically is that debate is a truth-seeking process. As the debate goes on, the human becomes better at answering correctly than answering wrongly. That's encouraging. As you get more persuasive debaters, as these LMs get better and more persuasive, it's even easier for the human to spot the right answer. That's really encouraging, because one failure case you could imagine is that as these LMs become more persuasive, the LM arguing for the wrong answer gets stronger at persuading the human and answering wrongly. But it's actually making it an even more truth-seeking process. Demonstrating this empirically with AIs as debaters was a really important contribution of this paper. We also show that even if it's not a human judge but an AI judge, this works: if an AI judge doesn't have access to the context and has to look at the two debates, even an AI is better at picking the correct answer over the wrong answer.

items.question: How do you see the potential of AI debate to combat misinformation generated by large language models?
items.object: AI debate as a way to combat misinformation
items.answer: I think that would be nice. I don't know, maybe that would be good. I think that's desperately needed. But the question with misinformation is also how receptive people are. Do people want to know longer debates and take the time to look through a debate, for and against a topic?
quotes: I think that would be nice. I don't know, maybe that would be good. I think that's desperately needed. But the question with misinformation is also how receptive people are. Do people want to know longer debates and take the time to look through a debate, for and against a topic?

rubrics.text: The response questions whether people would be willing to spend time reviewing extended debates as a way to address misinformation.

items.question: How do you think debate between language models could help overcome biases inherited from their training data?
items.object: Language-model debate as a way to overcome bias
items.answer:
That sounds like a great follow-up research project. My first hunch is that with two LMs, we have to keep in mind they're still trained on human data on the internet, and then there's the additional step of RLHF to become at least closer to what some hopefully less biased people think about the world. But even there, biases remain. The way we create these two debates is by taking a copy of the same LM but instructing it differently: one to argue for the correct answer, one to argue for the wrong answer. The biases these two debaters are going to have are the same ones. If they're both biased in a certain way, they probably won't disagree about that bias.

For that, you could imagine a multi-agent system of many different LMs trained on different subsets of the internet debating with each other. That might be an interesting future research project. The other one is to connect these models to some source of empirical evidence and let them actively seek information and question themselves, going back to the self-referential and self-improvement aspects. Maybe at some point they identify, “Do I have a bias on this? Let me investigate this further,” and look at data they can find online. Maybe that makes it worse. I don't know. Hopefully not.

items.question: How do you think about inference scaling as a way to expand what large language models can do?
items.object: Inference scaling and in-context learning in large language models
items.answer:
I think it makes a lot of sense. We're looking less and less into changing parameters of models and doing more and more in context. These large language models have a context window that you can use to prompt them or provide exemplary data, and that context window has been massively increasing over the last two years. Maybe two years ago a context window of 8,000 tokens was common; at some point maybe 20,000, 125,000. We are now at a stage where these models have a context window of two to 10 million tokens. That means they're not just conditioned on that many tokens; they can actually make use of what's provided in the context.

There's the needle-in-a-haystack experiment, where you can investigate to what extent models can retrieve specific information from a one- or two-million-token context. Two million tokens is massive. You can condition these models on a number of books or entire code bases. It's pretty mad to think about that. With that come a lot of possibilities for in-context learning, where the LM inside the context window can generate data, vary data, iterate until it produces an output. The things I mentioned, like Voyager, PromptBreeder, and Rainbow Teaming, all do interesting things without changing any model parameters; everything is happening in context. Same for the AI Scientist papers: they're not changing model parameters. The entire scientific loop is what we would call an outer loop to the LM.

items.question: Do you think we already have the components needed to build self-improving AI systems?
items.object: Self-improving AI systems built from foundation models, mutation operators, and selection operators
items.answer: I think all these things are in place. We have powerful foundation models, powerful mutation operators, powerful selection operators, and models that can code quite well. Putting this all together means we'll have systems, as I said, that self-improve based on empirical evidence that they collect in a number of hard domains. I think that's really what's going to drive further improvements in AI in the next few years. At least that's my personal view at this point.

items.question: How do you think about what AI might be capable of five years from now?
items.object: Forecasting AI capabilities over the next five years
items.answer: I usually struggle with this quite a bit because things are compressing so much. It becomes very hard to predict what's possible in half a year. With that in mind, on a time horizon of five years, I nowadays feel like anything is already possible.

items.question: Why do you expect the transition from human-level general AI to superhuman intelligence to happen quickly?
items.object: The transition from human-level general AI to superhuman intelligence
items.answer:
For the book I looked into Nick Bostrom's Superintelligence. One thing I found really funny in that book is that he talks about two surveys. One asked AI experts about their timeline until AGI will happen, and on average people said 20 years, which is always the answer they like to give when asked this question: just far enough. Really interestingly, they had a second survey asking the same people, given their previous answer, how long they thought it would take to get to artificial superhuman intelligence. I think the mean was another 20 or 30 years after that, which I find completely bizarre.

The moment you have a system that's generally capable at, let's say, human-level capabilities, specifically around coding and applying the scientific method, and enough compute to scale this up, the first thing you're going to do is apply this method to itself to self-improve. Shortly after, you have a superhuman system. I don't know exactly when we'll have a really strong, generally capable AI; this might be five to 20 years, whatever. But one thing I know is that once we have that, it's not going to take another 20 or 30 years until we have a superhuman intelligence system.

items.question: How do you assess predictions that AI will require a trillion-dollar compute cluster within a few years?
items.object: Predictions that AI will require a trillion-dollar compute cluster
items.answer: I don't know enough about this to have a really informed opinion at this point. The one thing I would say is that there are interesting opinions that, given current trends, we need a trillion-dollar compute cluster in a few years. But I think that's always taking current trends and extrapolating them on some kind of log scale, just fitting a linear. I'm assuming this is never how our technological breakthroughs happen. We're not really on an exponential that just goes on forever. As Yann LeCun said on Twitter, we usually have a concatenation of sigmoids that each lead to a new kind of locally exponential trend.
quotes: I don't know enough about this to have a really informed opinion at this point. The one thing I would say is that there are interesting opinions that, given current trends, we need a trillion-dollar compute cluster in a few years. But I think that's always taking current trends and extrapolating them on some kind of log scale, just fitting a linear. I'm assuming this is never how our technological breakthroughs happen. We're not really on an exponential that just goes on forever. As Yann LeCun said on Twitter, we usually have a concatenation of sigmoids that each lead to a new kind of locally exponential trend.

rubrics.text: The response characterizes predictions of a trillion-dollar AI compute cluster within a few years as extrapolations of current exponential growth trends.
The response proposes that technological progress follows a succession of sigmoid curves rather than a single indefinitely continuing exponential curve.

items.question: How do you think about compute technology as a constraint on AI progress over the next decade?
items.object: Compute technology as a constraint on future AI progress
items.answer: When making these predictions, I wouldn't assume that the compute technology we're using in 10 years is going to look anything like what we're using right now. It might be completely different and get us much further, who knows? But compute is definitely going to be at some point in the bottleneck for the next few years, for the kinds of things we discussed today.
